Starting with `@tanstack/react-query` v5.105.2, an inline `select` function that throws can cause an infinite render loop when the query component renders a stateful UI component.
React repeatedly renders the component until it reports:
The selector exception itself is caused by application data in this reproduction: the response omits an optional `result` field, while the selector calls `data.result.map(...)`.

I do not expect React Query to ignore the selector exception. I expect the query to enter an error state, or throw according to its error-handling options, without repeatedly updating the external-store snapshot.
The same reproduction is stable with v5.105.0 and v5.105.1. The loop starts with v5.105.2 and is still reproducible with v5.106.0.
4. Observe that v5.105.0 and v5.105.1 render a finite number of times.
5. Observe that v5.105.2 and v5.106.0 continue rendering until React reports `Maximum update depth exceeded`, or until the reproduction's observation window ends.
6. Observe that v5.106.0 no longer loops when the selector uses `data.result ?? []`.

If a `select` function throws, React Query should expose the selector error through the query result and settle without repeatedly forcing React to render. An unstable inline selector may run again on a later render, but it should not create its own render loop.

If the argument passed to a `useQuery` hook contains `NaN` anywhere, and the request returns an error, the hook dispatches the same query again in an endless loop. Each rejection causes a rerender, and each rerender dispatches a new request. The only thing pacing the loop is network latency, so a fast server gets hammered with hundreds of requests per second.

This is easy to hit in practice. Our case was a URL where a route param placeholder was never substituted, so the page received the literal string `""user_id""` and `Number(""user_id"")` produced `NaN`, which then flowed into a query arg. The server rejected the request with a 400 and the client retried it forever.

- With a mocked fetch that resolves instantly, we measured over 10,000 requests in about 200ms from a single mounted hook (no StrictMode, single subscriber).
- Unmounting the component stops the loop.
- The identical setup with a valid id (`{ id: 123 }`) receiving the exact same 400 response makes exactly one request. So the error is not the trigger. The `NaN` in the args is.

My application uses two different React renderers, the official React one and [react-pixi-fiber](https://github.com/michalochman/react-pixi-fiber).

These roots are nested within each other and share a store, there is a `<Provider>` at the top of each root, the store is passed in as a prop to the container of the nested root and then rendered into its `Provider` using `ReactDOM.render()`.

For the most part this works OK and connected components are notified in the correct order, however I am also using [redux-undo](https://github.com/omnidan/redux-undo) and for some reason whenever I dispatch one of its inbuilt actions (`UNDO` or `REDO`) then my connected components in the nested root update before their connected parents have had a chance to rerender, in the case where they would have no longer been rendered (they were deleted) I run into this issue.
Connected components always update after their connected parents have re-rendered.
After reading the article posted about the issue I am of the conclusion this is due to using two separate context providers for the same store (due to having multiple react roots).
I am also unsure as to why the correct order of updates appears to be maintained unless I am dispatching an action to [redux-undo](https://github.com/omnidan/redux-undo).
Short of writing defensive code I was wondering if it is possible to pass enough information from one context to the other so that the existing guards are effective?

549,GitHub,https://github.com/strapi/strapi/issues/27411,strapi/strapi,27411,"Admin login drops the refresh cookie when the admin panel is served from a different origin than the API, so the session can never be refreshed","### Node Version

When the admin panel bundle is served from a different origin than the API (`STRAPI_ADMIN_BACKEND_URL` / `window.strapi.backendURL` pointing at another host), the admin session can never be refreshed. The user is forcibly logged out at `accessTokenLifespan`, even while actively using the panel.
The cause is that the refresh cookie is never stored in the first place.
`packages/core/admin/admin/src/utils/getFetchClient.ts` sets `credentials: 'include'` on exactly one request — the token refresh:
credentials: 'include', // Include cookies for the refresh token

The regular `get` / `post` / `put` / `del` methods of the same client do **not** pass `credentials`, so they default to `same-origin`. Login goes through this path — `packages/core/admin/admin/src/services/auth.ts` defines the `login` mutation as `{ method: 'POST', url: '/admin/login' }`, which reaches `fetchClient.post` via `baseQuery`.

Per the Fetch specification, a response to a cross-origin request whose credentials mode is not `include` has its `Set-Cookie` ignored by the browser. `POST /admin/login` is what sets the `strapi_admin_refresh` cookie (`packages/core/admin/server/src/controllers/authentication.ts`), so in a cross-origin setup that cookie is silently discarded.
Login itself still succeeds, because the access token is returned in the response body. The breakage only surfaces later:
1. `useIdleSessionLogout` arms a renew timer shortly before the access token's `exp`.
2. The user is active, so it calls `POST /admin/access-token`.
3. That request *does* send credentials, but there is no `strapi_admin_refresh` cookie to send.
4. The server responds `401 Missing refresh token`.
5. `baseQuery` treats this as a dead session and logs the user out of every tab.

So the symptom is ""logged out after `accessTokenLifespan` (30 minutes by default) even while working"", and it is not fixable through `admin.auth.sessions` or `admin.auth.cookie` configuration — no cookie attribute can help a cookie that was never stored.

Note this is independent of `SameSite`. In our setup the two hosts are different origins but the *same site* (they share the registrable domain), so `SameSite=Lax` would happily send the cookie. The cookie simply does not exist.

When a tag has a falsy ID, it is treated as _without ID_ on writing, but as _with ID_ on read and cleanup.
- The tag is never effectivelly invalidated by such ID
- The stale query references accumulate (instead of being cleaned up after unsubscribe)
Codesandbox project: https://codesandbox.io/p/devbox/t5myq5 (please look at the [reproduction.js](https://codesandbox.io/p/devbox/t5myq5?file=%2Freproduction.js) source file)
My use case was using a numeric ID starting with zero, which is a falsy value. The same behavior happens when using an empty string as the tag ID.
Using `0` or `""""` (empty string) as a tag ID is a legal use based on the Typescript definition:
For a falsy tag ID, the following paths disagree:
1. Write path: `id || '__internal_without_id'` - falsy ID is regarded as tag without ID (packages/toolkit/src/query/core/buildSlice.ts)
2. Read path: `(tag.id !== undefined ? ... : ...)` - falsy ID (which is not undefined) is regarded as a valid ID (packages/toolkit/src/query/core/buildSelectors.ts)

3. Cleanup path: `tag.id ?? '__internal_without_id'` - falsy ID (which is not null/undefined) is regarded as a valid ID, so the original __internal_without_id bucket does not get cleaned up. (packages/toolkit/src/query/core/buildSlice.ts)

For consistency, the same policy should be used in all places regarding falsy values. A minimal fix is to use `tag.id ?? We have a blank React landing page to handle the redirects and intercepting of the data via the javascript postMessage bridge. A boolean flag is set to denote that the React app is being browsed via mobile native Webview in redux state, and then in a `useEffect` waiting for this flag to be set, the user is redirected to the intended page/route. Redirecting is a mix between utilizing react router and directly via `window.location`.

From my understanding, this is what's happening:

301,GitHub,https://github.com/TanStack/query/issues/11160,TanStack/query,11160,Stale `select` error from a previous query leaks into the next query's pending result,"## Describe the bug

When a `select` function throws, the error is stored on the observer (`#selectError`) and surfaced on every result. It is only ever cleared inside the select block itself — which is skipped entirely while `data` is `undefined` (`queryObserver.ts`, `createResult`). So after switching the observer to a different `queryKey` (or after `resetQueries`), the new pending query reports `status: 'error'` carrying the *previous* query's select error. With `throwOnError` or suspense, the stale error is thrown into the error boundary while the new query is still fetching.
Equivalent in React: `useQuery({ queryKey: ['user', id], ... })` where `select` throws for id ""a"", then setting id to ""b"".
Second repro without a key change: after the select error, call `queryClient.resetQueries({ queryKey })` — the reset pending state still carries the old select error.
While the new (or reset) query is fetching and has no data, the result should be `{ status: 'pending', error: null }`. A select error belongs to the data it was computed from
column2: once that data is gone, it should not leak into the next result.

column1: The cause is that `createResult` only clears `#selectError` on a successful select run inside the `options.select && data !== undefined` block
column2: the `if (this.#selectError)` check below it then fires unconditionally. Related but distinct from #11011 (which fixes `isPlaceholderData` when select throws on placeholder data).

When using `node-fetch` on Node.js 19+ to make two consecutive requests to the same web server, we always get the error: `FetchError: request to <URL> failed, reason: socket hang up`

> TLDR: This issue is caused by https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/47130 in nodejs, exacerbated by an issue with `node-fetch` blindly sending `Connection: Close` headers. This was fixed via #1736 in `node-fetch` v3.3.2 (note: 3.x is only ESM-enabled). This will hopefully be fixed in `node-fetch` v2 once #1765 is merged and released.

This error only arises with `node-fetch` and Node.js 19+ (tested using 19.9.0 and 20.0.0), and the web server we were using was Axum. We didn't see this issue when using a node-based proxy to help with debugging - I imagine it depends slightly on the order of TCP packet delivery and latency and the internal state machines of the HTTP servers - but it seems like many HTTP servers would see this issue.
The error appears to only occur where the **second request to the same server in the same round of the event loop as the first request was awaited**, which gives the error:
FetchError: request to <URL> failed, reason: socket hang up
We believe the following explains what we're seeing, and is backed up by logs at the end of this post:
* `fetch` sends a `connection: close` header in its first HTTP request...
* The server responds with a http response, which `fetch` hands back to the caller.

* The server actions the close connection request by following up the http response with a TCP packet with the `FIN` flag. This marks the end of the connection from the server's point of view. At this point, it does not expect to receive any further requests.
* Still in the same event loop, the caller calls fetch again to make its second HTTP request to the same origin.
* Node.js attempts to send the next request to the host using _the same connection_
* But the TCP connection is closed at the server's end, so returns a `conn reset` at the TCP layer
And I believe this may be the cause:

* The first response from the server is handed back to the caller likely in the [poll phase of the event loop round](https://nodejs.org/en/docs/guides/event-loop-timers-and-nexttick#phases-overview)).
* In the mean time, the server has responded to close the TCP connection - but the event loop doesn't get round to handling it (not least because it's not yet in the `close callbacks` phase)
* The caller then attempts to send a new request. But as far as the event loop is concerned, we're still at the `poll` stage, and haven't yet handled the socket close event...

* So I would guess that Node.js internally has yet to close the connection (because it's waiting for the `close callbacks` stage?), so attempts to send the HTTP request on the same (as yet unclosed) connection.

451,GitHub,https://github.com/socketio/engine.io/issues/279,socketio/engine.io,279,CORS pre-flight breaks socket.io behind load balancer,"I ran into an issue on our servers. We are running socket.io v1.0.6 on multiple server instances behind a load balancer. For polling, the requests go through the ELB with sticky sessions turned on. Our real-time service is on a subdomain, and thanks to CORS pre-flight requests, socket.io fucks up. Here is what happens on the client when the polling transport is used:
1. A socket.io handshake POST request occurs. The response comes back valid with an `sid`, and the headers include the AWS ELB cookie.

2. Next, a pre-flight `OPTIONS` request is made by the browser. The ELB cookie is _not_ included by the browser here. As a result, the `OPTIONS` request is routed to a potentially different server which will not recognize the `sid` in the query string.
3. When the request is routed to the wrong server, socket.io responds with a 400 HTTP status code and an `Session ID unknown` error.
4. Since the pre-flight request fails, the browser also fails the actual GET polling request, and tries to re-do the handshake from the beginning
5. Possibly due to the headers being sent, the browser sends the `OPTIONS` pre-flight request fairly regularly as opposed to doing it only once, so this cycle repeats over and over.

The fix on our end currently is to respond to all `OPTIONS` requests with a 200 and all the usual `Access-Control-Allow-…` headers the browser knows and loves. We do this before they even get to socket.io in our nginx config.
Now, engine.io appears to already handle this case here: https://github.com/Automattic/engine.io/blob/master/lib/transports/polling-xhr.js#L40
However, that check is only reached if the `sid` is valid here: https://github.com/Automattic/engine.io/blob/master/lib/server.js#L180

which it isn't, of course. I can submit a PR but I'd like to know how you guys think it'd be best to handle this. AFAIK, if a request method is `OPTIONS`, we can make the assumption that we are polling. But, since we don't have a valid `sid` to look up a client by, this might mean moving fairly transport-specific logic into `server.js` which sounds less than ideal.

`fetchQuery` may throw an `CancelledError { silent: true, revalidate: undefined }` under the following conditions:
- the query is stale (otherwise the fetch won't run).
- the query is invalidated at least one tick after the fetch started.
- **the query is in an `active` state. For example because a component with `useQuery` is still mounted.**

In the real world, this might happen in combination with `react-router`, when the user submits a form and then navigates to a new (or the same) page. In my case, we were updating a search param to close a modal after a form submission, which then triggered the loader function containing a `fetchQuery` call. We're also using a mutation observer[^1] to trigger invalidations, which is why the invalidation happened only after the navigation began.
I fixed the issue by using `ensureQueryData` instead of `fetchQuery`. This is the better choice anyways.

Still, this seems like a footgun since it is difficult to catch while testing. Further, if the intended behavior for `fetchQuery` is to throw a `CancelledError` on invalidation, it should *always* do that and not only when a revalidation is triggered.
Option A: The returned promise should _consistently_ reject, regardless of whether an unrelated observer exists.
Option B: The returned promise should _consistently_ resolve with the data returned from this fetch
Option C: The QueryClient should treat pending promises as observers, revalidate automatically and always resolve with the result from the latest revalidation.
